groups.label: Word Stress & Syllable Prominence
rules: Most 2-syllable nouns stress the first syllable (DOC-tor, TEA-cher).
-teen numbers stress the second syllable (thir-TEEN), -ty numbers stress the first (THIR-ty).

groups.label: Sentence Stress & Schwa /ə/
groups.definition: Prominence of content words and weak forms
rules: Content words (nouns, main verbs, adjectives) are stressed.
Function words are unstressed and often use the schwa sound /ə/.

groups.label: Suffix Stress Patterns
groups.definition: Predictable stress shifts caused by specific word suffixes
rules: Suffixes like -tion, -sion, and -ic place primary stress on the syllable immediately preceding them.
Neutral suffixes like -ful, -less, and -ly do not alter the root word's stress position.

examples.m: Unchanged stress root with neutral suffixes

groups.label: Stress-Timed Rhythm
groups.definition: Rhythmic structure where stressed syllables occur at regular time intervals
rules: English is a stress-timed language: the time between stressed syllables remains relatively constant regardless of how many unstressed words sit between them.
Unstressed syllables are compressed and spoken faster to maintain sentence beat.

examples.t: The CATS have been EATING the FISH ➔ 1... 2... 3...
examples.m: Same duration despite added functional words

groups.label: Compound & Functional Stress
groups.definition: Stress distinctions in compound nouns, phrasal verbs, and noun-verb pairs
rules: Compound nouns usually stress the first word (BLACK-board), while adjective + noun phrases stress the second word (black BOARD).
Noun-verb homographs stress the first syllable as a noun (EX-port) and the second as a verb (ex-PORT).

examples.t: GREEN-house (building for plants) vs green HOUSE (house painted green)
examples.m: Compound noun vs adjective phrase stress

groups.label: Stress Shifts in Word Families
groups.definition: Movement of primary stress across related derivatives of the same root word
rules: Adding derivational suffixes can shift primary stress to different syllables across a word family.
Vowel quality changes when stress shifts (stressed vowels become full, unstressed vowels become schwa /ə/).

groups.label: Secondary Stress & Stress Shift
groups.definition: Secondary stress marks in long words and stress retraction to avoid adjacent stress clashes
rules: Polysyllabic words often carry a secondary stress /ˌ/ in addition to primary stress /ˈ/ (e.g. /ˌɪntəˈnæʃnəl/).
When a word with final primary stress precedes a stressed noun, its stress shifts backward to avoid a stress clash (e.g., thir-TEEN ➔ THIR-teen MEN).

examples.m: Stress retraction to avoid stress clash

groups.label: Nuclear Stress & Pragmatic Focus
groups.definition: Location of the tonic syllable (nuclear stress) to signal discourse focus, presupposition, and contrast
rules: The tonic syllable (nucleus) defaults to the last content word of an intonation phrase, but shifts to signal contrast, correction, or narrow focus.
Given information receives low prominence, while new or contrastive information receives nuclear stress.

examples.t: John bought a BLUE car. (Default nucleus on last content word)
JOHN bought a blue car. (Focus on who bought it)
examples.m: Nuclear stress shift for pragmatic focus

groups.label: Rhetorical Prosody & Metrical Cadence
groups.definition: Manipulating stress distribution, rhythmic feet, and speech tempo for persuasive oratory
rules: Formal public speaking uses deliberate stress alignment, extended pauses, and rhythmic parallelism to enhance rhetorical impact.
Metrical variation creates emphasis by contrasting isometric stress cadence with sudden accelerations or decelerations.

examples.t: 'ASK NOT / what your COUNTRY / can DO for YOU'
'WE shall FIGHT on the BEACHES, / WE shall FIGHT on the LANDING GROUNDS'
examples.m: Anaphora reinforced by nuclear stress alignment
